forecasts.label: Interest payable

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Kent schools deficit stands at £130.5m, with £162.5m government grant agreed against it
news_drafts.lead:
Kent County Council's deficit on the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) stood at £130.5m at 31 March 2026, up from £97.5m a year earlier. The figures are in papers for the Governance and Audit Committee on 15 October. The council's external auditor reports that the government has approved a £162.5m grant covering 90% of the existing deficit, with adjustments for payments already made.

The deficit grew by 34% in 2025/26. Spending on high needs (school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities, SEND) overspent by £64.6m. After a £3.3m underspend on early years, the central schools reserve showed a net overspend of £61.8m. The council's Safety Valve agreement with the Department for Education, in place since summer 2022, ended on 31 March 2026. A High Needs Sustainability Grant, subject to an approved SEND reform plan, is due in autumn 2026 and is not counted in the 2025/26 accounts.

A statutory override, a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet, ends in March 2028. The auditor's interim report forecasts further deficits of £109.5m in 2026/27 and £137.6m in 2027/28, £247.1m together. It says the council lacks the working balances to cover them once the override ends. The council's Annual Governance Statement calls the deficit "the Council's most significant financial risk".

news_drafts.headline: Kent schools deficit forecast at £238.5m for 2026-27, with a £162.5m government grant awaiting approval
news_drafts.lead:
Kent County Council's deficit on the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools, here overspent mainly on support for children with special needs) is forecast to rise from £130.5m to £238.5m in 2026-27. The first-quarter budget report went to Cabinet on 1 October. It puts the overspend on high needs (the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities) at £109.2m for the year.

The forecast does not include a High Needs Stability Grant of £162.5m, announced in February 2026. The council applied in June 2026 and has not yet had a decision. The paper says the grant "depends on the Department for Education (DfE) approving a local Special Educational Needs & Disability (SEND) reform plan". A statutory override (a temporary government rule keeping such deficits off the main balance sheet) expires on 31 March 2028. From 2028-29, the government has stated an intention, not a guarantee, that councils will not have to fund these deficits from the General Fund, the council's main budget.

The council's quarterly performance report gives part of the explanation. It says 10.8% of pupils with education, health and care plans are placed in independent or out-of-county special schools, against a target of 9%. It attributes this to "delayed provision of two new special schools", leading to over-reliance on independent specialist places. The report says the Department for Education has recently confirmed the schools remain in its plans, but the measure "is likely to remain below target for the foreseeable future".

news_drafts.headline: Kent pension fund assets rise to £9.4bn but costs jump 39% in a year
news_drafts.lead: Kent's pension fund grew its assets by almost £1bn in the year to March 2026, reaching £9.4bn on the back of investment returns of 11.5%, outperforming its benchmark. The improvement lifted the fund's overall funding level from 102% to 104%, allowing contribution rates for most employers to fall. However, the fund's total costs—administration, governance and investment management combined—jumped by 39% over the same period, from £40.1m to £55.8m. Fund manager fees alone rose by roughly £2.5m due to higher asset valuations, particularly in equities. At the same time, annual benefit payments grew 6.3% to £353.5m, outpacing contribution growth. Over five years, benefits have risen 37% while pensioner numbers increased 18%, showing the fund is in a paying-out phase with proportionally fewer working members to spread the cost.

findings.headline: Monitoring Officer function resourcing reviewed due to increasing governance demands, complaint volume and LGR work
findings.detail: The Council has reviewed the resourcing of the Monitoring Officer function "in light of increasing governance activities, volume of complaints, and the work involved in providing governance advice connected with Local Government Reorganisation". The statutory Monitoring Officer functions are currently "undertaken by a small team". An action for 2026-27 is to review whether the function has "sufficient resources to carry out statutory function alongside the additional, specialist governance advice that will be required alongside the LGR process".
findings.matters: The Monitoring Officer is a statutory post with specific legal duties. If under-resourced, governance may suffer or the council may face risk of unmet statutory obligations. The review acknowledges this as a concern.
findings.figures: No specific staffing numbers provided; described as "small team"
findings.quote: The resourcing of the Monitoring Officer function is an area that has been reviewed in light of increasing governance activities, volume of complaints, and the work involved in providing governance advice connected with Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.headline: No Monitoring Officer Section 5 reports issued in 2025-26, a change from prior years' breaches on UASC matters
findings.detail: The Monitoring Officer did not issue any Section 5 reports under the Local Government and Housing Act 1989 during 2025-26. The paper notes this is "in contrast to earlier years, where there were a number of Section 5 reports presented in connection with breaches of statutory duties arising from Kent County Council's involvement in judicial review proceedings relating to the care of unaccompanied asylum-seeking children (UASC)".
findings.matters: Section 5 reports indicate the council has breached statutory duties. The absence of such reports, particularly given prior years' issues on UASC care, suggests resolution or improved control of those specific risks. This is positive governance news compared to the prior situation.
findings.quote: The Monitoring Officer, during the period of this Audit up to the time of writing, has not issued a Notice pursuant to s. 5 of the Local Government and Housing Act 1989.

findings.headline: Implementation of agreed audit management actions improved to 61-64% in 2025-26 from 34% in 2023-24
findings.detail: The rate at which the council implements agreed management actions to address audit findings has risen substantially. In 2023-24 it was 34%; by 2024-25 it had reached 62%; in 2025-26 it was 64% (January) and 61% (July). The paper describes this as "a positive step" to be "built upon in 2026-27".
findings.matters: Implementation rates show whether the council acts on its own audit findings. Improving rates suggest the council is disciplined in addressing identified control weaknesses. This is a positive governance trend.
findings.quote: In 2024-25, full implementation rates increased to 62% in 2024-25 from 34% in 2023-24. The positive trend in implementation of agreed management actions was taken into 2025-26 with implementation reported to January (64%) and July (61%) Governance and Audit Committees.

findings.headline: Internal Audit opinion of Adequate Assurance maintained since 2019-20, but with increased Limited assurance areas
findings.detail: Internal Audit assigns "Adequate Assurance" to corporate governance, risk management and internal control overall. This opinion is consistent with ratings since 2019-20. However, the proportion of systems/processes assigned "Limited" assurance increased to 17% in 2025-26 from 15% in 2024-25. Positively, 50% of systems received "Substantial" or "High" assurance (maintained from prior year).
findings.matters: Adequate assurance is the middle of the assurance scale. The increase in Limited assurance areas warrants monitoring. The maintained Substantial/High rate is positive. Finance directors track audit opinion trends as indicators of control effectiveness.
findings.figures: Adequate assurance overall; 50% Substantial/High (unchanged); 17% Limited (up from 15%); maintained since 2019-20
findings.quote: Internal Audit concludes that Adequate Assurance can be assigned in relation to the Council's corporate governance, risk management and internal control arrangements... There has been a maintained trajectory in the proportion of systems, processes or functions which are assigned an assurance level of "Substantial" or "High" with 50% in 2025-26 in line with 50% in 2024-25... There was a slight increase in the assigning of "Limited" assurance in 2025-26 to 17% from 15% in 2024-25.

findings.headline: Government paused Local Government Reorganisation on 7 September 2026 after announcing 4-unitary option on 16 July
findings.detail: The Government initially decided on 16 July 2026 to proceed with Option 4B (four new unitary authorities for Kent and Medway), with shadow elections planned for May 2027 and vesting day 1 April 2028. However, on 7 September 2026, the Government announced a review of the LGR programme and confirmed plans for Kent and Medway would be "paused". The paper describes the scale, complexity and timing of LGR requirements as "already having, and will continue to have, a significant impact on the operating position and capacity of the Council".
findings.matters: LGR creates major organisational uncertainty. A pause after months of preparation is costly in terms of staff distraction, planning resources, and creates new risks. Lenders need to know about major structural uncertainty affecting the council's future direction and stability.
findings.figures: Option 4B announced 16 July 2026; pause announced 7 September 2026; shadow elections were to be May 2027; vesting day 1 April 2028
findings.quote: On 16 July 2026, the Government announced its decision to proceed with Option 4B for Kent and Medway, which would establish four new unitary councils... However, on 7th September 2026 the Government announced a review of its Local Government Reorganisation programme and confirmed that plans for Kent and Medway will be "paused" while that review is carried out.

daily_post.headline: Adult Social Care Older People services overspent by £8.9m; residential care unit costs and community support usage above budget.
daily_post.lead: Adult social care is a large cost base (£786.7m budget, 47% of General Fund) with inelastic demand. Rising unit costs and usage pressures here indicate demographic and social care market pressures that are structural and likely to recur.
